title: WAF safelist experiments and synthetic-traffic hypotheses (oncall notes)
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a working log of short-lived WAF safelist experiments run from 2026-02-14 -> 2026-02-28 and a set of on-call hypotheses and tactical playbook notes for handling traffic floods and suspected API key leakage. The intent is tactical: reduce customer-impacting false positives while creating reliable signals for automated throttling and key rotation triggers. Not a finalized runbook — keep conservative until we have post-experiment validation.

Background / why this mattered this week:
- On 2026-02-12 we saw a spike of high-rate requests against the hosted API proxies (10x baseline) where source IPs were concentrated around two ASN blocks. Latency SLOs degraded on several routes and customers reported 429s.
- Initial mitigation (global WAF blocklist) reduced traffic but caused collateral customer errors; postmortem flagged over-broad IP blocks.
- Aim of experiments: (1) test short-duration safelists scoped to known customer CIDR ranges to avoid blocking legitimate traffic during tuning, (2) evaluate fingerprinting heuristics to separate synthetic/fuzz traffic from legitimate bursts, (3) identify robust signals that should auto-trigger key rotation / playbook escalation.

Experiment summary (high-level):
- Experiment A: Scoped safelist by customer CIDR + rate-limited exception window
  - Window: 15 min, scope: customer-cidrs only (derived from account metadata), rate cap: burst 500 requests/min per API key, global cap still enforced.
  - Purpose: avoid blocking legitimate customer retries during upstream bursts.
  - Result: reduced customer 429s by ~62% during windows. But abuse traffic that appeared to use valid keys still consumed tokens; downstream costs rose ~9%.

- Experiment B: Temporary safelist for healthcheck and monitoring agents only
  - Scope: IPs with reverse-DNS matching common monitoring providers + User-Agent allowlist.
  - Result: negligible impact on attack surface; eliminated a small portion of false positives but not material.

- Experiment C: WAF dynamic fingerprinting + adaptive throttle
  - Fingerprint features: abnormal seq length, token distribution entropy, request inter-arrival distribution, missing typical headers (Accept-Language), repeated prompt templates.
  - Throttle policy: initial soft-throttle (50% token rate) + challenge (captcha-like token exchange) for suspect clients; escalate to hard throttle on continued pattern.
  - Result: detected ~78% of synthetic traffic in labeled test corpus; real-world throughput reduced with low customer impact. False positive rate estimated ~2.7% (needs more validation).

Key observations and signals that mattered:
- ASN clustering alone is insufficient; legitimate customers sometimes route through shared gateways (CDNs, cloud ISPs). Combine ASN + CIDR ownership (account metadata) to decide safelist.
- API key reuse across geographies correlated strongly with abuse; when the same key used from >3 distinct /16s within 5m we saw high likelihood of compromise.
- User-Agent and header heuristics are brittle but useful as low-cost signals for prioritization.
- Billing/usage spikes often lag attack onset; use token-consumed rate and immediate tokenized request rate (requests/sec) as leading indicators.

Quick detection queries (kept here for oncall):
- Kibana request query (approx):
  event.dataset:proxy AND request.path:/v1/generate AND NOT http.response.status_code:[200 TO 399] AND response.bytes:>0 | group by api_key, client_ip, geoip.country
- BigQuery (token burn detection):
  SELECT api_key, count(*) as reqs, sum(tokens) as tokens, approx_top_count(client_ip)
  WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 10 MINUTE) GROUP BY api_key HAVING tokens > 100000
- GCP logging (example):
  gcloud logging read "resource.type=global AND jsonPayload.route=/v1/embeddings AND jsonPayload.requestCount>1000" --limit=50

Tactical playbook (short checklist for noisy-key or flood detection):
1) Rapid triage (first 10 min):
   - Identify top 5 API keys by tokens and request rate (10m window).
   - Cross-check API key owner, last seen geo, and recent config changes (Console audit logs).
   - If API key shows >3 distinct /16s in 5 minutes: mark as compromised candidate.
2) Immediate mitigations (first 15–30 min):
   - Apply per-key soft throttle: limit to 20% of observed peak and add leakage marker tag in telemetry.
   - If traffic persists or spikes again, escalate to forced rotation: generate new key and rotate via api (notify owner via email+console).
   - If many customers affected (widespread): consider region-scoped dynamic WAF rule with conservative thresholds and an explicit monitoring window.
3) Customer communication & CS handoff:
   - Use templated message (CS) informing about suspected compromise, mitigation steps taken, and how to rotate keys.
   - Provide temporary bypass if customer proves ownership and needs continuity (issue a short-lived token via support flow).
4) Post-incident review actions:
   - Gather sample request payloads (store in secure bucket), fingerprints, and timeline.
   - Run offline ML classifier on labeled set; tune fingerprint thresholds to target <1% FP.

Runbook snippets / commands to run during incident:
- List top API keys by tokens (Kusto/BigQuery): see detection query above.
- Rotate a compromised key (infra tool): infra-cli keys rotate --key-id <key> --reason "suspected_leak"
- Apply temporary WAF rule (gcloud): gcloud compute security-policies rules create --security-policy=proxy-waf --expression='ip.src in cidrList("x.y.z.0/24")' --action=allow --priority=9000 --description='temp safelist test'
- Enable dynamic profiling for an API key (internal feature flag): toggles in console -> key -> enable-fingerprint-profiling

Open questions / TODOs (from experiments):
- How to measure customer-impacted latency and 429s accurately per route during short windows? Need a dashboard that overlays WAF rule changes with per-route error rates. (JIRA-SRE-4538)
- Determine safe default for soft-throttle percentage. Experiment C used 50% — consider 25% in next window.
- Decide on automatic vs human-in-the-loop for forced key rotation. Current legal/CS policy prefers human approval for enterprise accounts. Document exceptions.
- Build a canonical CIDR ownership mapping service (account metadata) to avoid overbroad ASN blocks. (blocked by infra pruning of account metadata sync)

Notes from on-call debrief (2026-02-18):
- Samir: default WAF blocking caused three paying customers to file escalations; avoid global blocklist without account mapping.
- Jordan: fingerprinting early-detection reduced noise—next step is to push a low-latency scoring path into the edge proxies.
- Ivy: add a playbook section for legal/forensics to preserve evidence (S3 bucket ACLs, retention).

Proposed next experiment (short):
- 72-hour rolling window where we:
  a) enforce per-key soft throttle at 30% on keys matching suspect fingerprint score >= 0.85
  b) allow exceptions for keys with CIDR ownership matching account metadata
  c) collect false positives via customer feedback channel and auto-label dataset
  d) daily review by oncall for escalation decisions

Appendix (notes / heuristics):
- Suspect fingerprint score heuristic (informal):
  score = 0.4*(geoip_entropy_score) + 0.3*(token_entropy_score) + 0.2*(ia_rate_score) + 0.1*(header_absence_score)
  threshold used in experiment: 0.85 for suspect; 0.65 for low-confidence watchlist.
- Helpful links:
  - Incident runbook canonical: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Incident+Runbooks
  - Customer rotation docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/keys#rotate

Raw logs & artifacts location (internal):
- s3://redwood-sre/incident-logs/2026-02-waf-safelist-experiments/

If you're reading this and plan to run the next window: annotate the document with experiment start/end timestamps and update the results section immediately after. Keep this doc lightweight and iterative.

-- Talia
